title: McBoyle v. United States (1931)
summary: A criminal statute that lists land vehicles and then adds "any other self-propelled vehicle not designed for running on rails" does not reach airplanes, because the words must give fair warning in language ordinary people understand.
notes: Supreme Court of the United States, 1931. Key line: "It is a vehicle that runs, not something, not commonly called a vehicle, that flies." (Justice Holmes)

sections.Parties: The petitioner, McBoyle, was the defendant convicted in federal court of transporting a stolen airplane across state lines. The respondent was the United States, which prosecuted him under the National Motor Vehicle Theft Act of 1919. Counsel for McBoyle argued that the statute's list of vehicles was borrowed from state motor-vehicle statutes in Connecticut, Delaware, Ohio, Michigan and Missouri and from the District of Columbia traffic regulations, none of which dealt with anything that leaves the ground. The government defended the conviction on the theory that an airplane is a self-propelled vehicle not designed for running on rails.
sections.Material Facts: McBoyle flew an airplane that he knew had been stolen from Ottawa, Illinois, to Guymon, Oklahoma. He was convicted under section 3 of the National Motor Vehicle Theft Act, which punishes whoever transports in interstate or foreign commerce a motor vehicle knowing it to have been stolen, and was sentenced to three years in prison and a $2,000 fine. Section 2(a) of the Act says the term "motor vehicle" shall include "an automobile, automobile truck, automobile wagon, motor cycle, or any other self-propelled vehicle not designed for running on rails." Airplanes were well known in 1919 when Congress passed the Act, but it was admitted that they were never mentioned in the committee reports or the floor debates.
sections.Procedural History: McBoyle was tried and convicted in federal district court of transporting a stolen airplane in interstate commerce and received a three-year sentence and a $2,000 fine. He sought review, and the Supreme Court granted a writ of certiorari limited to one question: whether the National Motor Vehicle Theft Act applies to aircraft. The Supreme Court answered that it does not, and the conviction could not stand under that statute. The opinion for a unanimous Court was written by Justice Holmes.
sections.Issue: Whether the word "vehicle" in the catch-all phrase "any other self-propelled vehicle not designed for running on rails," following a list of automobiles, automobile trucks, automobile wagons and motor cycles in the National Motor Vehicle Theft Act, includes an airplane, so that knowingly transporting a stolen airplane across state lines is a federal crime under the Act.
sections.Holding: No. The Act does not apply to aircraft. In everyday speech "vehicle" calls up the picture of a thing moving on land, and the carefully enumerated list of land vehicles confirms that reading. A criminal statute should not be extended to conduct its words do not clearly describe merely because a similar policy seems to apply or because Congress probably would have used broader words had it thought of airplanes. Congress must give fair warning in language the common world understands.
sections.Reasoning: Holmes conceded that "vehicle" can etymologically cover conveyances on land, water or air, and that some statutes use it that way. But ordinary usage pictures something that moves on land. The statutory context confirms the popular meaning: after listing automobile truck, automobile wagon and motor cycle, the general phrase "any other self-propelled vehicle not designed for running on rails" still takes land travel as its theme. This is ejusdem generis reasoning, though Holmes did not use the label: general words at the end of a specific list are read as things of the same kind. The exclusion of rail vehicles makes sense only if land vehicles are the subject. The phrasing was borrowed from state motor-vehicle statutes that never contemplated aircraft, and Congress never mentioned airplanes though they were well known in 1919. Holmes then stated the rule of lenity in its fair-warning form: although a criminal rarely reads the statute before acting, the law should draw a clear line in language the public understands, and a court should not extend a criminal statute to new conduct on speculation about what the legislature would have wanted. There was no dissent.

topics.lrs-k-lenity: Holmes grounds lenity in fair warning: a criminal prohibition must be stated in words the common world understands, so a court does not extend it to conduct the words do not plainly describe.
topics.lrs-k-ejusdem: The general phrase "any other self-propelled vehicle" takes its meaning from the preceding list of automobiles, trucks, wagons and motor cycles, all of which run on land.
topics.lrs-k-textualism: The Court reads the enacted words in their ordinary sense and refuses to expand them on speculation that Congress would have used broader language had it thought of airplanes.
topics.lrs-k-legislative-history: Holmes notes that airplanes were never mentioned in the reports or debates, treating that silence as confirming rather than supplying the statute's meaning.
topics.lrs-k-canons: McBoyle shows two canons pointing the same way, ordinary meaning reinforced by the list, and states the policy behind lenity as fair notice rather than tenderness to defendants.

learning.separateOpinions: None. Justice Holmes wrote for a unanimous Court.
learning.why: The case teaches the rule of lenity in its fair-warning form and an early use of ejusdem generis: a general catch-all following a specific list of land vehicles is confined to the same class, and a criminal statute is not stretched to cover airplanes on the guess that Congress would have wanted it to.
